Anthropic's Claude goes local in India
articles.summary: Anthropic has brought in-country inference for its Claude AI models to India through Amazon Bedrock, allowing prompts and model responses sent through its India endpoint to be processed on servers located within the country.The move is aimed at addressing data-residency requirements for regulated sectors, giving enterprises a way to keep sensitive AI workloads within India while using Anthropic’s Claude models.Also Read: Anthropic IPO prospectus reveals deep reliance on Amazon, Google for sales and computeIn practical terms, when an Indian customer uses the India endpoint, the prompt sent to Claude and the model’s response are processed on servers in India. Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Web Services’ platform for accessing and deploying generative AI models, provides the infrastructure through which customers can access Claude locally.Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5 are now available with in-country inference through Amazon Bedrock in India.India is Anthropic’s second-largest market for Claude.ai, with software development accounting for 45.2% of work-related tasks that users bring to Claude in the country, the highest share of any market, said Irina Ghose, managing director at Anthropic India, in an interview with TOI.The company’s adoption in India has also spread beyond software development, with businesses across banking and payments, large enterprises, IT services, digital companies, healthcare, science and public services using Claude.TCS is equipping 50,000 associates with Claude, while Infosys is combining the model with its Topaz platform. Cognizant uses Claude in systems it builds for clients, while LTTS is embedding the technology into its engineering platforms.For these businesses, the ability to process AI workloads within India could be particularly important where data handling and regulatory requirements restrict how sensitive information can be processed.Also Read: Anthropic targets more than $2 trillion valuation in closely watched IPO despite $42 billion 2025 loss"Requests sent to Claude through the India endpoint are processed on servers located within India. That is what our customers in India, especially in regulated sectors, asked us for: to use Claude on their most critical work with every request processed within the country," Ghose said.Financial institutions, government bodies and large enterprises had sought local inference because of regulatory and data-handling requirements, she added.The availability of local inference could also allow some deployments that had been waiting for the capability to move forward, Ghose said.The India expansion comes as Anthropic looks to deepen its presence in a market where enterprise adoption of generative AI is widening and where data localisation and residency requirements are becoming increasingly important for large organisations.For customers with sensitive workloads, the India endpoint provides a way to use Claude while keeping the processing of those requests within the country.

articles.title: The numbers behind US midterms
articles.summary: Washington: Americans go to the polls on November 3 for elections that will shape the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency -- although the president himself will not be on any ballot.The "midterms," held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide control of Congress as well as governorships and thousands of state-level offices.Also Read: US midterm elections: Trump stumps for candidates in deep red Alabama and says he'll be back again next weekA Democratic takeover of either chamber would constrain Trump's agenda and bring greater congressional scrutiny of his administration; Republican victories would preserve the party's control in Washington.Here is a look at the 2026 showdown by the numbers:- House of Representatives -435: Every seat in the House, the lower chamber of Congress, is contested every two years.218: The magic number for a majority in the 435-seat chamber.3: The net number of seats Democrats need to gain from the 2024 election result to take control. Republicans won a 220-215 majority then, although deaths, resignations and a party switch mean the current House stands at 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.For Republicans, that means a net loss of two seats is survivable. Three is not.- Senate and the states -35: Senate seats being contested -- 33 in the normal six-year rotation plus special elections in Florida and Ohio.Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage in the 100-seat chamber, counting two independents who vote with the Democrats. Democrats therefore need a net gain of four seats to reach the 51 required for control; a 50-50 tie would be broken by Republican Vice President JD Vance.36: States electing governors, nearly three-quarters of the total.6,139: State legislative seats being regularly contested, across 88 of the country's 99 state legislative chambers.- What the polls say -53-41 percent: The Democratic advantage over Republicans among registered voters asked which party's congressional candidate they would support, in a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll conducted September 14-15.The same survey found Democrats ahead among independent voters by 57 percent to 32 percent.32-41 percent: The range of Trump's approval rating in several major September surveys.Also Read: US midterm elections: 9 key issues that could shape the November pollsReuters/Ipsos put him at 32 percent among US adults, the lowest of his political career, while Marist recorded 39 percent and NBC News 41 percent among registered voters. The surveys use different methodologies and populations, so the figures are not directly comparable -- but none suggests an abundance of presidential coattails.55 percent: Registered voters who told NBC News that Trump's policies had hurt the economy, against 26 percent who said they had helped it.- Money, money, money -About $12 billion: The amount expected to be spent advertising on the 2025-26 election cycle.Ad-tracking company AdImpact forecasts $11.6 billion, exceeding both the previous midterm record of $8.9 billion in 2022 and even the 2024 presidential cycle.Kinetiq Political Insights' latest estimate is slightly higher at $11.96 billion, with a projected range of $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion.$330 million: Advertising spending in the California governor's primary alone, according to AdImpact -- making the preliminary contest to choose November's candidates the most expensive gubernatorial race on record.And that was merely the warm-up.- For the trivia file -2,497: Candidates who ran in US congressional primaries this year, the most in any election cycle since at least 2014. An extraordinary 2,232 of them were chasing House seats.44: House races on November 3 that are rematches between the same major-party candidates who fought for the seat in 2024.Broaden the search to state and local contests and there are 474 electoral rematches nationwide -- proving that in American politics, as in Hollywood, there is rarely any objection to a sequel.

articles.title: UAE shared FlyDubai flight details with Israel
articles.summary: Tel Aviv, Israel: Authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it, regional officials said Sunday, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later told the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel."With the investigation into the FlyDubai incident underway, preliminary details have highlighted several major security lapses. Officials already have said the Omani co-pilot had been barred from flying by his own country because of concerns about his extremist views. It also remains unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly a planeload of Israelis to Tel Aviv.The UAE, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight's captain with the cockpit's crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a "terrorist attack" Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to rush in and subdue the attacker.Israel did not raise concerns about passengers and crewThe regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities. Israel hadn't raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters about the probe.The Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev on X said the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn't given a list of passengers or any warnings.Sharing the list is standard aviation procedure. But the head of aviation security at the Transportation Ministry, Dvir Rubenstien, told Army Radio that the ministry relies on local security checks and does not have the tools or the ability to run checks on each passenger on every flight.Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don't maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.Australian police said Sunday that counterterrorism investigators were looking into the attacker's possible connections to Australia, where media have reported he went on a student visa to study at university about a decade ago. The Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology said Monday he was enrolled at the school for a time but did not successfully complete an engineering qualification.The passengers who halted the attack and helped regain control of the aircraft have been hailed as heroes in Israel.Questions being raised about security failuresBut as the initial euphoria of the rescue has subsided, officials have begun to raise difficult questions and trade accusations about the security blunders that could have led to a major disaster.Ahead of the elections at the end of the month, some opposition candidates have seized on the security failures to highlight what they perceive as negligence on the part of Netanyahu and his supporters. Transportation Minister Regev is a member of Netanyahu's Likud party and a staunch supporter."This is exactly what system collapse looks like," Yair Golan, head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. "A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security."It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk.Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared."In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks," he said.

articles.title: Next-gen GST to boost growth, ease compliance
articles.summary: India's ambition to become a Viksit Bharat requires an economy in which enterprises of every size can grow, wherever they begin. Over the past 12 years, our government has worked to create those conditions. GST's introduction in 2017 established a common national framework for indirect taxation. Next-gen GST carries that effort forward, drawing on nine years of implementation and the experience of taxpayers and states.Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision, next-gen GST was conceived with two connected purposes: to reduce and rationalise rates, and to make compliance easier. The rate changes took effect on September 22, 2025. The next phase of process reforms will come before the GST Council shortly. Together, these efforts seek to give households relief, businesses greater certainty and taxpayers a system in which they can fulfil their obligations without avoidable difficulty.Also Read: GST 2.0 may scrap arrest powers, raise prosecution barStates have been partners throughout. They brought their priorities and experience to the council, helped shape the decisions and undertook their implementation. I thank them for that commitment.The results provide grounds for confidence. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the value of reported taxable supplies grew 25.8% over the corresponding period a year earlier. A lighter rate structure has been accompanied by a substantial expansion in reported economic activity. This is an encouraging foundation for a reform intended to support both enterprise and public finances.Also Read: India within reach of 8% growth, says Ex-RBI guvThat resilience is visible in the latest revenue figures. Gross GST collections reached ₹12.46 lakh crore during April-September 2026, up 11.6% from a year earlier. Every month from June through September recorded double-digit annual growth; together, collections for these four months accelerated by nearly 15%. Net collections, after refunds, grew 10.4% over the half-year. Taxpayer relief has coexisted with growth in the resources available for development.The breadth of the expansion matters as much as its scale. Reported taxable supplies grew across all 11 sector groups and all major states. Growth across sectors and regions creates opportunities for more businesses to participate in expanding markets, and for more communities to benefit from the demand, investment and employment that follow.Reported sales to consumers (B2C) rose 26.7% in the post-reform comparison. When tax relief is reflected in prices, families have more room to meet other needs or save. Consumer relief and enterprise growth are closely connected: the purchasing power of households sustains demand for the goods and services that businesses provide. The benefits can extend from the household to the retailer, the supplier and the producer.For small and medium enterprises, a national market is valuable when it opens a practical route to customers beyond their immediate surroundings. Businesses in tier-2 and tier-3 towns should be able to build those relationships while continuing to invest and employ people locally. Enterprises expanding into these towns, in turn, can create opportunities for local suppliers and distributors. GST's common framework supports these connections; simpler administration must make them easier to sustain.Participation in that framework is substantial. GST registrations across central and state jurisdictions were about 17.1 million at the end of August, up nearly 15% from a year earlier. For the April-July 2026 tax periods, GSTR-3B returns filed by their due dates were 12.6% higher. These improvements place a corresponding responsibility on the administration: regular compliance must be supported by reliable service, clear guidance and timely resolution of difficulties.The functioning of input tax credit is another important part of this experience. The post-reform figures show that the share of tax liability discharged through credits rose, while accumulated credit declined relative to taxable supplies.This is encouraging for businesses that depend on the effective use of eligible credit. For a smaller firm, working capital determines how readily it can purchase inputs, fulfil an order and take on the next one. Refunds are equally relevant. About ₹1.80 lakh crore was refunded during April-September. Returning amounts due to businesses is part of a well-functioning tax system. Greater predictability in this process would help enterprises plan purchases and production with more confidence.(The writer is the union minister of finance and corporate affairs.)

articles.summary: New Delhi: India should build its own artificial intelligence (AI) safety framework suited to its languages, scale, and application-led AI ecosystem rather than replicate a voluntary pact signed by US President Donald Trump and top technology firms last week, industry experts said.They also called for a commitment that brings together all stakeholders and tackles risks such as deepfakes and cyberattacks, even as they differed on whether voluntary measures alone would be enough.The comments came after the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a voluntary AI safety pact signed on September 29 by Trump and top executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Nvidia and Elon Musk's xAI.Under the accord, the companies committed to internal controls to monitor their AI models, dedicated oversight teams, independent external audits and board-level oversight. They also agreed to meet regularly to set safety standards.Nasscom Chairman and Fractal Group CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said India should not simply replicate the US. Instead, it should use a domestic commitment as a building block towards a global understanding of AI safety."As models become more capable and agentic, we are giving them greater access to systems and greater autonomy to make decisions. AI safety must be strengthened considerably and must stay ahead of capability to prevent catastrophic risks," Velamakanni said.He noted that the US accord is largely a push for self-policing by frontier AI companies. The European Union, by contrast, has taken a binding, risk-based approach, while China follows a state-directed control model.India, the Nasscom Chairman said, could use its role in the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) and the momentum from hosting the AI Impact Summit in February to prevent worst-case outcomes, without citizens of India and the Global South being denied access to frontier models."India doesn't need to copy the US model, but it can take inspiration from it and expedite efforts to build a trusted AI ecosystem," said Soumen Mandal, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research.He added that such a commitment should cover testing AI systems before deployment, independent audits, reporting serious problems, and naming people responsible for AI-related risks.Amit Khanna, Partner and Automation Ecosystem Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat, said any commitment should be suited to Indian market conditions.He noted that India's focus is on building AI applications rather than major foundational models."An industry commitment in India should ensure AI works reliably across vernacular languages and unique cultural contexts and should not exploit AI knowledge asymmetry in the population," Khanna said.Ganesh Gopalan, co-founder and CEO of Gnani.ai, said any framework must ensure a level playing field.Global frontier models should be subject to the same rules as Indian ones, he said, since Indian AI companies compete with global firms for the same customers.The experts differed on whether self-regulation would be enough."Voluntary, self-regulatory approaches are necessary but woefully insufficient," Velamakanni said."Pharmaceuticals and aviation are great examples of industries where strong, technically competent regulators have strengthened safety and public trust without stopping innovation."He said India needs binding rules on transparency, incident reporting, and accountability when serious harm occurs.The IndiaAI Safety Institute should be strengthened to test newly released models, but without creating a bottleneck by requiring pre-release certification of every model, he added.Mandal backed a hybrid approach. Mandatory rules would apply to potential harms in defence, healthcare, banking, and government use cases, while voluntary standards would cover fast-moving technical areas where regulators may lack technical expertise."This type of hybrid approach will provide flexibility to AI companies instead of restricting every line of code while ensuring safety and privacy are not compromised," he said.Khanna also called for a hybrid "techno-legal" approach. It would pair a strong voluntary layer with binding mandates, such as the provisions on synthetically generated information in the IT Amendment Rules, 2026.He said voluntary compliance alone leaves significant gaps, particularly in civil rights and public safety.Gopalan, however, favoured self-regulation."Voluntary self-regulation is key given the technology is new. Having mandatory regulation can stifle competition and lead to concerns about a few companies getting preferential treatment."India needs more than 100 frontier AI lab companies, and that's the need of the hour to prevent India from being colonised, which is inevitable if we lag behind in the AI race," Gopalan said.The Indian government is in the process of bringing in its own AI regulation.Earlier this year, IT Secretary S Krishnan noted that while existing legal provisions have so far been adequate in addressing initial concerns on issues like deepfakes and AI-generated synthetic content, an "additional regulation or law may be needed"."It is a conversation which has commenced, and my minister (IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw) and I have both been on record earlier that we will look at AI regulation when the time is right, and it appears that the time is getting right, and we will start looking at it," he had said.Vaishnaw had also said that the current information technology law was framed much before the rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and that a new legal framework may be required to deal with the changing landscape.The industry agrees that any pact should go beyond AI companies."This cannot be an agreement among AI companies alone," Velamakanni said.He said the government, frontier model developers, large deployers, including enterprises and public agencies, academia, and independent safety researchers should all have defined roles. Workers, users, and civil society should have formal channels to report harms.He added that safety evaluations of frontier models should be carried out by independent, expert institutions and published, with narrow exceptions where disclosure itself creates a security risk.Mandal said the agreement should bring together the entire AI ecosystem, from AI companies and their business users to regulators, universities, researchers, workers, and users.Khanna argued that it should include government and public sector bodies, which would be major users of AI, as well as civil society, worker unions, and technology companies.Meanwhile, Gopalan called for broader self-regulation across the AI ecosystem to ensure impartial access to limited compute resources.Velamakanni said the top concern must be preventing catastrophic and systemic harms.He listed large-scale cyberattacks, electoral interference, biological or chemical weapons, attacks on critical infrastructure, and loss of control over highly autonomous systems. Individual harms such as deepfakes, fraud, impersonation, privacy breaches, and self-harm come next."Autonomy must lag behind assurance to provide a margin of safety. As AI systems gain the ability to act in the world (use tools, move money, change systems, make consequential decisions), the evidence that they are safe and controllable must grow faster than the autonomy we give them," he said.Gopalan said that given India's large population and democratic framework, the bigger concerns are deepfakes and cyberattacks targeting financial institutions.Khanna also named deepfakes as the top immediate priority.He described misinformation, deepfakes, and political manipulation as "existential threats to India's social fabric".He said rules on liability when AI systems fail, such as misdiagnosing a patient or wrongly denying welfare benefits, remain a critical gap.Mandal placed independent audits first, followed by accountability, data protection, deepfakes, and job impact."Without independent testing and audits, the system will not be complete, as companies may sometimes overlook AI-related concerns," he said.

One in seven women worldwide suffers from endometriosis, a painful condition more common than diabetes that robs years from women's working lives, though much of the damage is avoidable, a medical expert said.
Prolonged disease can lead to infertility, as it damages the ovaries and fallopian tubes, while the resulting inflammatory environment hampers implantation, endometriosis surgeon and Indian Centre for Endometriosis (ICE) director Dr Abhishek Mangeshikar told PTI.

articles.title: Steel Ministry asks SAIL, NMDC to explore overseas mineral assets

The Steel Ministry has asked its undertakings, SAIL and NMDC, to explore mineral assets abroad to help secure long-term raw material requirements and support input costs, an official said.
Steel Authority of India Ltd (SAIL) is India's largest public sector steel-making entity, and NMDC is the country's leading iron ore player.
On a query on whether steel PSUs, especially SAIL and NMDC, have been asked to look for mining assets abroad, the senior ministry official replied in the affirmative.
The move will help secure future requirements and reduce cost, the official said without sharing further details.
Iron ore and coking coal are two basic raw materials needed to produce steel, besides limestone and pulverised coal injection (PCI Coal), among others.
While iron ore is available in abundance in the country, Indian steel makers, including SAIL, remain heavily dependent on imports for 85-90 per cent of their coking coal requirements from countries such as Australia and Mozambique.

articles.title: Cornell faces a Greek life reckoning
articles.summary: Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus following an outcry over the school's handling of a student's rape allegations, the Ivy League school's president said on Saturday.A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman, who alleges she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has sparked outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the school in Ithaca, New York.Also Read: What happened at Cornell University? The allegations, conflicting accounts and probe now underwayIn a video message, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future. That includes "a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," Kotlikoff said."At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community," he said. "But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility."The university will seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to "preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of others."The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish some of the accused students.The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times reported.Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.Also Read: New York governor appoints special prosecutor in Cornell fraternity rape caseBut "we must do better," Kotlikoff said. "We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves."He vowed that university officials would "be more transparent" about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but he did not detail specific initiatives that the university would take."In the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our community to ask questions and hear directly from university leadership," he said.The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect ​them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.

Yemen-Houthi conflict flares again
articles.summary: Sanaa: Yemen's internationally recognised government on Saturday (local time) confirmed strikes against what it described as "vital targets" of the Houthis in Sanaa and Saada, after the rebel group claimed it carried out a missile and drone operation targeting Aramco facilities in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh.The developments mark a fresh escalation in the ongoing conflict, with both sides issuing statements claiming military actions.Also Read: Saudi Arabia plans assault on Houthis to break Red Sea chokeholdIn a statement issued by the media centre of the Armed Forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government, the official spokesperson said Yemeni forces were carrying out strikes against Houthi-controlled areas."We are delivering painful strikes against vital targets of the terrorist Houthi militia in Sanaa and Saada," the official spokesperson said.The spokesperson further warned that Houthi military capabilities would remain under attack."The capabilities of the Houthi militia will not be safe from the fire of our armed forces, and we will destroy them," the spokesperson added.The statement came after the Houthi group said it had launched a military operation targeting Aramco in Riyadh using ballistic missiles and drones.According to a statement issued by Houthi military spokesperson Brigadier General Yahya Saree, the attack was carried out in response to what the group described as Saudi strikes against Sanaa and other areas under its control."In response to the Saudi aggression against the capital, Sana'a, and the liberated provinces, which in the past 24 hours reached up to 60 airstrikes and missile attacks, bringing the total number of Saudi aggression attacks since the escalation against our country to 1,410," the Houthi statement said.The Houthi group said that it carried out a "qualitative military operation" using ballistic missiles and drones against Aramco facilities in Riyadh.Also Read: Saudi-led coalition says Houthis targeted power station in MedinaThe group claimed that the operation achieved its objective and said fires broke out at the targeted sites."The operation successfully achieved its objective, thanks to Allah," the statement said."The strikes were precise and direct, resulting in fire breaking out at the targeted sites," it added.The Houthi statement also warned of further escalation, saying the group would respond to what it described as attacks against Yemen and its people."The shedding of Yemeni blood with such criminality and brutality necessitates that the armed forces, along with all the free people of our nation, take all necessary escalatory steps and deterrent measures to affirm to everyone that the price for disregarding the blood of our faithful people will be high and exorbitant, and the criminal enemy must understand that continuing to shed our people's blood will cost them dearly," the statement said.The group further said it would continue its policy of escalation until the attacks and blockade against Yemen end."We will continue to impose the equation of "a siege for a siege", and "an escalation for escalation", and targeting the Saudi enemy's troop buildups until the aggression ceases and the siege on our beloved country is lifted," the statement said.The latest exchange of strikes comes amid continuing tensions involving Yemen's internationally recognised government, the Houthi group and Saudi Arabia, with both sides accusing the other of escalating military action.
